quotes.text: An interval `[start, end]` includes both endpoints and every point between them. Thus `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` share the point `2` and must become `[1,3]`. `[1,2]` and `[3,4]` have a gap and remain separate. Integer endpoints do not turn the intervals into sets of integers; the gap between `2` and `3` still matters. A single-point interval such as `[12,12]` is valid.

LeetCode 56 accepts between `1` and `10^4` intervals. Each has exactly two integer endpoints satisfying `0 <= start <= end <= 10^4`. Input order is not promised. The result must have no overlapping intervals while covering exactly what the input covers. Adding points in a gap would be incorrect.

Think of coverage as the collection of all points included by at least one interval; mathematicians call this the union. Two input lists are equivalent for this task when their unions are equal. Their original order and repeated copies do not affect the union.

The statement does not promise that callers want their input rearranged or edited. The implementation below therefore preserves both the input list's order and its inner pairs. It returns new pairs. It also returns `[]` for an empty input, though empty input lies outside the stated constraints.
Once starts move only to the right, a new interval beginning after the current stretch ends proves that all later intervals also begin too far right to reach that stretch.

Use a list named `merged` for the components found so far. Its pairs are ordered by start and separated by strict gaps. The last pair is the frontier: it may grow when the next interval arrives. Earlier pairs are complete.

Connections through a chain are what justify the single merged interval `[1,4]`. Keeping the component's furthest endpoint retains the information needed for the next connection, even after the original members have been forgotten.

quotes.text: A loop invariant is a statement that remains true at the same checkpoint on every iteration. Here the checkpoint is immediately before processing the next sorted pair. At that point, `merged` is an exact, fully merged description of the processed prefix: it has the same union, starts increase, and every neighboring output pair has a strict gap. All pairs except possibly the last are final even with respect to unread input.
Initially the processed prefix and `merged` are both empty. They cover no points, and there are no pairs whose ordering or gaps could violate the invariant.
In Python, `sorted(intervals, key=lambda pair: pair[0])` returns a new outer list.
A new outer list does not mean new inner pairs. Its entries still refer to the input pair objects.
The right endpoint must mean the furthest reach of the entire current component. It cannot mean merely the previous input interval's end.

`for start, end in ordered` reads a pair and binds its two values to the local names `start` and `end`. `merged[-1]` selects the last output pair; the following `[1]` selects that pair's end. Assigning to `merged[-1][1]` replaces that slot in the existing pair. It neither appends another component nor replaces the entire output list.

For the first interval, `not merged` is true because `merged` is empty. Python's `or` stops after a true left operand, so the expression never tries to index the nonexistent last pair. On later iterations it tests the gap.

Instead, `merged.append([start, end])` creates a fresh two-item list for each new component. The integers can be shared safely because the program never changes an integer object; it replaces an entry in an output pair. The input pairs are only read.

quotes.text: Sort by increasing start instead.
For the first interval, `not merged` is true because `merged` is empty. Python's `or` stops after a true left operand, so the expression never tries to index the nonexistent last pair.

Let the current stretch be `[left, right]`, and the next sorted interval be `[start, end]`. Sorting gives `left <= start`. If `start <= right`, the intervals meet or overlap. Their union has no hole, begins at `left`, and ends at `max(right, end)`. If `start > right`, points between `right` and `start` are uncovered. Preserve the current stretch and start a new one.
Instead, `merged.append([start, end])` creates a fresh two-item list for each new component.
Assigning to `merged[-1][1]` replaces that slot in the existing pair. It neither appends another component nor replaces the entire output list.
Every unread interval has a start at least as large as `start`; none can fill this newly established gap from the left. The old last component can now join the earlier final components.

The loop has consumed every pair. `return merged` returns `[[1,10],[12,14]]`; no final flush is required because the frontier has already lived in the output throughout the scan. The return value shares neither its outer list nor its inner pairs with the input.

quotes.text: Initially the processed prefix and `merged` are both empty. They cover no points, and there are no pairs whose ordering or gaps could violate the invariant.

For maintenance, suppose a next pair `[start,end]` arrives. If the output is empty, a fresh copy represents exactly that first pair. Otherwise, sorting guarantees that `start` is no earlier than the start of the last component. If `start` is no greater than its end, the intervals intersect. Replacing that end by their maximum represents their exact union: it adds precisely the new covered points and leaves no hole. Its left endpoint stays fixed, so it cannot disturb the gap to an earlier component.

If `start` is greater than the last end, appending preserves both exact coverage and a strict gap. Every unread interval has a start at least as large as `start`; none can fill this newly established gap from the left. The old last component can now join the earlier final components. These cases preserve the invariant.

Suppose an earlier component ends at `a`, and the last component begins at `b`, with `a < b`. Every new start is at least `b`. It therefore cannot reach backward across that gap into the earlier component. If it reaches any saved component, only the last one is a candidate. This removes the need to rescan the whole output after each interval.
Equal starts need no secondary endpoint order for this algorithm: either order will be combined by the maximum.

Instead, `merged.append([start, end])` creates a fresh two-item list for each new component. The integers can be shared safely because the program never changes an integer object; it replaces an entry in an output pair. The input pairs are only read.

At termination the processed prefix is the entire input. The invariant supplies exact coverage and strict gaps between output components. Thus no pair of output intervals overlaps, and no covered point has been lost or invented. The loop terminates because it visits each element of a finite sorted list once.
no final flush is required because the frontier has already lived in the output throughout the scan.

answers.answer: 正文定義 n 為 input intervals 數、k 為 output components 數且 k<=n；Big O 是忽略固定倍數等的成長上界，不是秒數。endpoint<=10^4 使其大小有界，comparison/indexing/entry replacement 視為 constant；key 每 pair 一次，共 O(n)；scan n 次、每次固定 tests/reads/max，總共有 k 次 append。append 單次可能搬移 references，但 CPython v3.14.0 按目前大小比例預留容量；正文以 geometric progression 與倒看固定比例遞減說明總搬移量受最終容量固定倍數限制，k 次合計 O(k)，亦解釋 amortized 是整段序列上界。排序以 runs 合併的概念模型說明：每輪倍增大小，約 log2(n) 輪，每輪線性工作，因此最壞 O(n log n)，並明說真實 CPython schedule 更複雜但保有此上界；log2(8)=3 的倍增例有解釋。加上 key/scan 得總最壞 O(n log n)，n=1 為 constant。output 有外層 list 和 k 個固定雙元素新 pair，O(k)；排除 input/output 的 auxiliary 仍 O(n)，因 ordered n references，加 sort keys/merge temporaries；scan 自己只持固定 local references。peak extra O(n+k)=O(n) 由 k<=n 得。in-place list.sort 只省 outer copy，並無 O(1) sorting auxiliary 保證；已排序版本移除 sorting 後 O(n)，streaming 用一 pending pair O(1) working state，但 consumer 或 returned list 的 k results 仍占 O(k)。正文的 caveats 對 runs、log2、geometric progression、amortized、working/output space 都有本地說明，未發現為重建上述成本所必需而缺少的概念定義。CPython 具體上界為正文所述，這裡不開來源獨立驗證實作。

quotes.text: Let `n` be the number of input intervals and `k` the number of output components, so `k <= n`. Big O gives a growth bound while ignoring fixed multipliers and small fixed overhead. `O(n)` means work bounded by a constant times the input size; `O(n log n)` includes an additional factor that grows as a logarithm. These are operation-count statements, not elapsed seconds.

Treat endpoint comparison, indexing and replacing a list entry as constant work here. The statement bounds endpoints by `10^4`, so these integers have bounded size. The sorting key reads one endpoint per pair, contributing `O(n)` work. The scan visits `n` pairs; each visit makes a fixed number of tests, reads and maximum comparisons, plus at most one append.

An append can occasionally require a larger storage area and copying existing references. It is not correct to claim that every individual append costs constant time. In CPython v3.14.0, list storage grows with spare capacity proportional to its current size. Across repeated growth, copied capacities form a geometric progression: viewed backward, earlier capacities decrease by a fixed fraction. Their sum is bounded by a fixed multiple of the final capacity. Thus all `k` appends together cost `O(k)`, called amortized constant cost per append. This is a bound over the sequence, not an assumption that an occasional expensive append never happens.

CPython v3.14.0 uses an adaptive merge sort: it finds ordered stretches, called runs, and combines them. To see where the logarithm comes from, consider the conceptual case of combining equal-sized runs. A round doubles run size: `1, 2, 4, 8, ...`. Reaching `n` needs about `log2(n)` rounds; `log2(8) = 3` because three doublings turn `1` into `8`. Combining runs examines at most a linear number of items across each round, giving `O(n log n)` work. CPython uses a more elaborate merge schedule rather than those exact rounds, while retaining the worst-case `O(n log n)` bound. Existing ordered runs can reduce its work. This is a cost explanation, not a claim that the implementation literally splits every input into single items.

Adding sorting and the scan gives worst-case `O(n log n)` time for growing `n` (with constant work at `n = 1`). The visible single loop does not make the entire function linear: `sorted` performs its own work before that loop.

The returned result occupies `O(k)` space: one outer list and `k` fresh pairs, each of fixed size two. Excluding the input and returned result, auxiliary space is still `O(n)`. `ordered` contains `n` references, and sorting can keep keys and temporary merge storage proportional to `n`. Those temporary structures disappear after sorting, while `ordered` survives through the scan. The scan itself needs only a constant number of local references in addition to output. Peak extra space including the returned result is `O(n + k) = O(n)`. Using in-place `list.sort` would remove the copied outer list but would not justify a general `O(1)` auxiliary-space claim for CPython's sorting.

If a changed contract guarantees nondecreasing starts, remove the sorting call and scan that order directly. The same proof applies because its required ordering premise is now supplied by the caller. Time becomes `O(n)` under the same primitive-cost assumptions.
That version needs `O(1)` working state beyond its input stream and whatever the consumer stores. If the API still demands a returned list, storing the `k` results still needs `O(k)` space.

This also permits streaming: keep just one pending `[left,right]` pair, extend it when intervals meet, and emit it when a strict gap appears. Emit the last pending pair when input ends. Emission means passing a completed pair to a consumer instead of keeping all completed pairs in a list. That version needs `O(1)` working state beyond its input stream and whatever the consumer stores. If the API still demands a returned list, storing the `k` results still needs `O(k)` space.

The guarantee is essential. An unsorted stream might deliver a bridging interval after a component has been emitted; `[[5,6],[1,2],[2,5]]` already demonstrates the failure. For arbitrary input under the original contract, sorting is the chosen alternative to repeatedly revisiting previously saved components. The cost of arranging intervals buys the ability to finish each component once.

Why sort by start? Sorting makes future starts nondecreasing. Once a new start exceeds the current end, no later interval can bridge the gap.

Why keep the maximum end? The last output pair represents a whole connected component. A contained interval must not shorten its furthest reach.

Why does equality merge? The intervals are closed. Two intervals with a shared endpoint intersect at that point.

What is your invariant? Before each iteration, the output is the fully merged union of the processed prefix, ordered with strict gaps. Earlier components are final; only the last may grow.

What are the costs and mutation effects? Worst-case time is `O(n log n)`, auxiliary space is `O(n)`, and returned output uses `O(k)` space. The implementation preserves the input and creates new output pairs.
